::: {.solutions}

**18 questions.** Suggested time: **80 minutes**, no calculator.

Every question comes from a TMUA past paper, a TMUA mock, the MAT or the official Notes on Logic and Proof, and its
source is shown beside the question number. None of them appears in the S7 class questions.

For every question the routine is the same: **read one line at a time and ask whether it follows for every value the
line above allows.** Test a value in the original before you trust an answer, and remember that the honest verdict is
sometimes "no error".

| Section | What it covers | Questions |
|---|---|---|
| **A — Solving an equation: roots gained and roots lost** | squaring, cancelling, and a solution chain that loses or invents a value | 1–5 |
| **B — Inequalities and signs** | which operations keep an inequality, and which do not | 6–10 |
| **C — Proofs that do not hold up** | finding the first false line, or deciding that the proof is fine | 11–18 |

# Section A — Solving an equation: roots gained and roots lost

## Question 1 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">TMUA early specimen · P2 Q3</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following attempt to solve an equation. The steps have been numbered for reference.

$$\sqrt{x+5}=x+3$$
$$\text{step (1)}\ \big\downarrow$$
$$x+5=x^{2}+6x+9$$
$$\text{step (2)}\ \big\downarrow$$
$$x^{2}+5x+4=0$$
$$\text{step (3)}\ \big\downarrow$$
$$(x+4)(x+1)=0$$
$$x=-4\ \text{ or }\ x=-1$$

Which one of the following statements is true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** Both $-4$ and $-1$ are solutions of the equation.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** Neither $-4$ nor $-1$ are solutions of the equation.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** One solution is correct and the incorrect solution arises as a result of step (1).

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** One solution is correct and the incorrect solution arises as a result of step (2).

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** One solution is correct and the incorrect solution arises as a result of step (3).
:::

## Question 3 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2018 · P2 Q9</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following attempt to solve the equation $4x\sqrt{2x-1}=10x-5$:

$$4x\sqrt{2x-1}=10x-5$$
$$\text{(I)}\ \big\downarrow$$
$$4x\sqrt{2x-1}=5(2x-1)$$
$$\text{(II)}\ \big\downarrow$$
$$16x^{2}(2x-1)=25(2x-1)^{2}$$
$$\text{(III)}\ \big\downarrow$$
$$16x^{2}=25(2x-1)$$
$$\text{(IV)}\ \big\downarrow$$
$$16x^{2}-50x+25=0$$
$$\text{(V)}\ \big\downarrow$$
$$(8x-5)(2x-5)=0$$
$$\text{(VI)}\ \big\downarrow$$
$$\text{The solutions of the original equation are } x=\tfrac58 \text{ and } x=\tfrac52.$$

Which one of the following is true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** The solution is correct.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** Only one of $x=\tfrac58$ and $x=\tfrac52$ is correct and the error arises as a result of step (II).

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** Only one of $x=\tfrac58$ and $x=\tfrac52$ is correct and the error arises as a result of step (III).

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** Only one of $x=\tfrac58$ and $x=\tfrac52$ is correct and the error arises as a result of step (IV).

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** There is another value of $x$ that satisfies the original equation and the error arises as a result of step (II).

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** There is another value of $x$ that satisfies the original equation and the error arises as a result of step (III).

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** There is another value of $x$ that satisfies the original equation and the error arises as a result of step (IV).
:::

## Question 4 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2017 · P2 Q4</span>

::: {.question}
The following question appeared in an examination:

> Given that $\tan x=\sqrt3$, find the possible values of $\sin 2x$.

A student gave the following answer:

> $\tan x=\sqrt3$ so $x=60^\circ$ and $2x=120^\circ$, therefore $\sin 2x=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$.

Which one of the following statements is correct?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ is the only possible value, and this is fully supported by the reasoning given in the student's answer.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ is the only possible value, but the reasoning given should consider other possible values of $x$ for which $\tan x=\sqrt3$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ is the only possible value, but the reasoning given should consider other possible values of $x$ for which $\sin 2x=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ is **not** the only possible value because the reasoning given should have considered other possible values of $x$ for which $\tan x=\sqrt3$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** $\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ is **not** the only possible value because the reasoning given should have considered other possible values of $x$ for which $\sin 2x=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$.
:::

## Question 5 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2019 · P2 Q6</span>

::: {.question}
A student attempts to solve the equation

$$\cos x+\sin x\tan x=2\sin x-1$$

in the range $0\le x\le 2\pi$. The student's attempt is as follows:

$$\cos x+\sin x\tan x=2\sin x-1$$

So $\;\cos x-\sin x+\sin x\tan x-\sin x=-1$ &nbsp;&nbsp;**(I)**

So $\;(\sin x-\cos x)(\tan x-1)=-1$ &nbsp;&nbsp;**(II)**

So $\;\sin x-\cos x=-1\;$ or $\;\tan x-1=-1$ &nbsp;&nbsp;**(III)**

So $\;(\sin x-\cos x)^{2}=1\;$ or $\;\tan x=0$ &nbsp;&nbsp;**(IV)**

So $\;2\sin x\cos x=0\;$ or $\;\tan x=0$ &nbsp;&nbsp;**(V)**

So $\;x=0,\ \tfrac{\pi}{2},\ \pi,\ \tfrac{3\pi}{2},\ 2\pi$ &nbsp;&nbsp;**(VI)**

Which of the following best describes this attempt?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** It is completely correct

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** It is incorrect, and the first error occurs on line (I)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** It is incorrect, and the first error occurs on line (II)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** It is incorrect, and the first error occurs on line (III)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** It is incorrect, and the first error is that extra solutions were introduced on line (IV)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** It is incorrect, and the first error is that extra solutions were introduced on line (V)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** It is incorrect, and the first error is not eliminating the values where $\tan x$ is undefined on line (VI)
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:8cm"}

:::

# Section C — Proofs that do not hold up

## Question 11 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Tyler TMUA Set C · P2 Q5</span>

::: {.question}
A student attempts to prove the following statement.

> Consider the integers $a$ and $b$, where $a$ has remainder $1$ when divided by $3$, and $b$ has remainder $2$
> when divided by $3$. Then $a+b$ is always divisible by $3$.

Consider the following attempt:

&nbsp;&nbsp;Let $a=3n+1$ and $b=3n+2$ &nbsp;&nbsp;**(I)**

&nbsp;&nbsp;then $\;a+b=3n+1+3n+2$ &nbsp;&nbsp;**(II)**

&nbsp;&nbsp;so $\;a+b=6n+3$ &nbsp;&nbsp;**(III)**

&nbsp;&nbsp;so $\;a+b=3(2n+1)$ &nbsp;&nbsp;**(IV)**

&nbsp;&nbsp;therefore $a+b$ is always divisible by $3$. &nbsp;&nbsp;**(V)**

Which of the following best describes this proof?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** The statement is true and the proof is completely correct.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** The statement is true but there is an error in the proof in line (I)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** The statement is true but there is an error in the proof in line (II)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** The statement is not true and there is an error in the proof in line (III)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** The statement is not true and there is an error in the proof in line (IV)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** The statement is not true and there is an error in the proof in line (V)
:::

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** The statement is true but there is an error in the proof in line (IV)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** The statement is true but there is an error in the proof in line (V)

## Question 14 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Notes on Logic and Proof · Exercise O, Q1</span>

::: {.question}
Here is the proof that $\sqrt2$ is irrational.

> We assume that $\sqrt2$ is rational. Then it can be written as a fraction in its lowest terms, $\sqrt2=\dfrac ab$,
> where $a$ and $b$ have no factors in common. Squaring both sides gives $2=\dfrac{a^{2}}{b^{2}}$, which gives
> $2b^{2}=a^{2}$. From this we can see that $a^{2}$ is even. For $a^{2}$ to be even, $a$ itself must be even. And if
> $a$ is even then $a^{2}$ is divisible by $4$. If $a^{2}$ is divisible by $4$ then $b^{2}$ must also be even. For
> $b^{2}$ to be even, $b$ must be even. Thus, we have $a$ is even and $b$ is even. This contradicts the assumption
> that $\dfrac ab$ is a fraction in its lowest terms.

Replace $2$ by $9$ in the proof that $\sqrt2$ is irrational. Why does the proof no longer work?
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 15 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2020 · P2 Q8</span>

::: {.question}
A student is asked to prove whether the following statement $(*)$ is true or false:

$$(*)\quad\text{For all real numbers } a \text{ and } b,\quad |a+b|<|a|+|b|$$

The student's proof is as follows:

> Statement $(*)$ is false. A counterexample is $a=3$, $b=4$, as $|3+4|=7$ and $|3|+|4|=7$, but $7<7$ is false.

Which of the following best describes the student's proof?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** The statement $(*)$ is true, and the student's proof is not correct.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** The statement $(*)$ is false, but the student's proof is not correct: the counterexample is not valid.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** The statement $(*)$ is false, but the student's proof is not correct: the student needs to give *all* the values of $a$ and $b$ where $|a+b|<|a|+|b|$ is false.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** The statement $(*)$ is false, but the student's proof is not correct: the student should have instead stated that for all real numbers $a$ and $b$, $|a+b|\le|a|+|b|$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** The statement $(*)$ is false, and the student's proof is fully correct.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}

:::

## Question 16 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2023 · P2 Q4</span>

::: {.question}
A student attempts to answer the following question.

> What is the largest number of consecutive odd integers that are all prime?

The student's attempt is as follows:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; There are two consecutive odd integers that are prime (for example: $17,\,19$).

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; Any three consecutive odd integers can be written in the form $n-2,\ n,\ n+2$ for some $n$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; If $n$ is one more than a multiple of $3$, then $n+2$ is a multiple of $3$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**IV** &nbsp; If $n$ is two more than a multiple of $3$, then $n-2$ is a multiple of $3$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**V** &nbsp; The only other possibility is that $n$ is a multiple of $3$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**VI** &nbsp; In each case, one of the integers is a multiple of $3$, so not prime.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**VII** &nbsp; Therefore the largest number of consecutive odd integers that are all prime is two.

Which of the following best describes this attempt?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** It is completely correct.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** It is incorrect, and the first error is on line I.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** It is incorrect, and the first error is on line II.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** It is incorrect, and the first error is on line III.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** It is incorrect, and the first error is on line IV.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** It is incorrect, and the first error is on line V.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** It is incorrect, and the first error is on line VI.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** It is incorrect, and the first error is on line VII.
:::

## Question 18 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2017 · P2 Q9</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following attempt to prove this true theorem:

> *Theorem:* $a^{3}+b^{3}=c^{3}$ has no solutions with $a$, $b$ and $c$ positive integers.

*Attempted proof:* Suppose that there are positive integers $a$, $b$ and $c$ such that $a^{3}+b^{3}=c^{3}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; We have $a^{3}=c^{3}-b^{3}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; Hence $a^{3}=(c-b)(c^{2}+cb+b^{2})$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; It follows that $a=c-b$ and $a^{2}=c^{2}+cb+b^{2}$, since $a\leqslant a^{2}$ and
$c-b\leqslant c^{2}+cb+b^{2}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**IV** &nbsp; Eliminating $a$, we have $(c-b)^{2}=c^{2}+cb+b^{2}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**V** &nbsp; Multiplying out, we have $c^{2}-2cb+b^{2}=c^{2}+cb+b^{2}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**VI** &nbsp; Hence $3cb=0$ so one of $b$ and $c$ is zero.

But this is a contradiction to the original assumption that all of $a$, $b$ and $c$ are positive. It follows that the
equation has no solutions.

Comment on this proof by choosing one of the following options:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** The proof is correct

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** The proof is incorrect and the first mistake occurs on line I.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** The proof is incorrect and the first mistake occurs on line II.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** The proof is incorrect and the first mistake occurs on line III.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** The proof is incorrect and the first mistake occurs on line IV.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** The proof is incorrect and the first mistake occurs on line V.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** The proof is incorrect and the first mistake occurs on line VI.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:7cm"}
Working
:::
